label: Input/encoding window: original-phase steps from t=2 through the <DEL> step
explanation: Positional/phase feature. Fires on essentially every original-phase step from the third token (t>=2) through the delimiter step (rate ~0.9-0.99 at orig_idx 2-8, 0.96 at <DEL>), and is silent at t=0, almost silent at t=1 (0.9%), and nearly silent in the copy phase (0.1% of copy steps, ~0 mass). Token-agnostic in which token is input. Magnitude is modulated by content: highest activations occur when early original tokens are f, p, or q (first_tok f/p/q and prev2_tok f/p/q carry disproportionate mass; top examples all begin with f/p/q), peaking at the <DEL> step; repeated tokens (in_first=0) fire much less often (rate 0.09 vs 0.67). Activation also tapers at late positions in long sequences (rate 0.18 at t=9), the main source of false positives.

issues: The predicate and label hold up. (t>=2)&(t<=L) scores precision 0.946, recall 0.997, F1 0.971 and mass recall 0.9996 on the test split. Missed activations total 7,831 test steps and carry about 0.0% of the mass: weak firing at t=1 and scattered tiny copy-phase activations (rate 0.001). The label matches the predicate without overclaiming.

Claim refuted: 'Repeated tokens (in_first=0) fire much less often (rate 0.09 vs 0.67)'. Inside the window, (t>=2)&(t<L)&(in_first==0) has precision 0.972, so repeated tokens fire about 97% of the time. First occurrences (in_first==1) fire at 0.938. The 0.09 figure comes from the copy phase, where in_first is almost always 0 and the feature is silent anyway. Being a repeat does not suppress firing.

Claim refuted: 'Activation drops off at late positions in long sequences (rate 0.18 at t=9), which accounts for most of the false positives'. By orig_idx the firing rate rises with position: 0.897 (2), 0.912 (3), 0.957 (4), 0.982 (5), 0.988 (6), 0.982 (7), 0.956 (8). The low rate at t=9 appears because most t=9 steps are in the copy phase for L<9. False positives actually concentrate at the EARLY window positions t=2 and t=3, the opposite of what the explanation says.

Missing from the explanation: whether the feature fires depends on which tokens started the sequence, not only on how strongly it fires. Window precision is about 1.0 when orig(0) is a,b,d,f,p,q,s,u,0,1,3,m,o. It falls to 0.77-0.93 when orig(0) is e,g,h,i,j,k,l,r,t,v,w,y (w 0.768, j 0.828, e 0.832, r 0.848). That shortfall is largest at t=2 (0.75) and t=3 (0.79) and has almost recovered by t=5 (0.955). So the statement 'Which token is being input does not change whether it fires' holds for in_tok but not for the sequence's opening tokens.

Supported but overstated: the f/p/q magnitude effect is real. When first_tok is f, p or q, the window has precision 1.0 and holds 21.8% of the mass on 10.5% of active steps. 'Activation peaks at <DEL>' is weak, though. Mass per step is about flat from orig_idx 4 through <DEL> (about 4.1-4.6e-7 per step in each bin).
No better binary predicate found. Even the worst subsets (bad orig(0) at t=2) still have precision of about 0.75, so excluding them costs more recall than it gains in precision.
